The band bit with a tiny electronic flare across bone and tendon — a polite warning that tasted like lightning in his teeth. Somewhere above, the old intercom system clicked once — metallic, empty. Just the soft pop of a microphone live and waiting. He looked up, expression flat. “Doctor.” A snarl wrapped in civility. No answer. He meandered through the hallway slowly. At the doorway to the locker room, the cuff pulsed again — one quick shock that wasn’t pain so much as intrusion, a shiver that scraped the edge of every nerve. He staggered a half step before catching himself on the frame. “Childish.” He rubbed the wrist until sensation returned. The speakers exhaled a whisper of static, like the sound of breath filtered through glass. The quiet reasserted itself; the hum dropped away. He lowered himself to a bench, unwilling to show how much the jolt had burned. When he finally let his eyes close, the band cooled, almost gentle. For a few breaths he almost believed the experiment had paused. A low hiss: a faint pneumatic sigh under the metal. It wasn’t enough to cripple — just a drift of cold through the veins, a chemical whisper that left his thoughts too sharp and his body too heavy. A cheeky denial of rest. Wesker inhaled through the sensation, anger rolling up through him slow and black. This intrusion on his life had gone on long enough. Trying for a more subtle approach, he tried to work the virus under his skin as a wedge; to have Uroboros pry at the connection from within. The infection liked to be useful; it liked resistance. For a second he felt the tiniest give — a microscopic loosening in the cuff’s adhesive bite — and his heart stuttered at the thought of finally getting leverage as he pushed harder. Uroboros responded instantly, veins bulging as oily tendrils writhed up under the skin. The virus coiled around the band like a serpent, lashing at the flush-seated metal, bubbling where it touched — but each strike ended in recoil. It couldn’t grip. Couldn’t burn. Couldn’t bite. He snarled. Again. Harder. The infection swelled, pushing heat and pressure into the wrist until the skin trembled with strain. The band retaliated not with brute force but with bureaucracy. A soft injection hissed under the cuff edge — a gust of cool fluid, a bitter chemical bloom that stabbed at his vision and left organs humming with the taste of copper and bile. The cuff’s micro-sensors read the change and closed within milliseconds, a calibrated clamp that tightened an internal cycle of small, escalating shocks and a nausea-inducing cascade of neuromodulators. The world tipped sideways, stomach reeling from the assault even as his virus ate through the chemicals. He turned, grabbed his combat knife from the locker bench, and pressed the tip against the faintest ghost of a seam in the band — a trick of the light, maybe. Hopefully, just enough. The cuff sparked red. The shock tore down his arm, a precision strike against the nerves that set his heart lurching unsteadily against his ribs. The knife jumped from his fingers with a clatter, hand spasming so violently it left his wrist half-numb. Uroboros hissed inward like steam into a vacuum, retreating from the bone as if it had been scalded. He’d never be able to hold the combat knife steady enough to try again, not with how hard his hand vibrated from the aftershock. He glared at the band, breathing heavier now. The band had progressed from a mere insult to an outright challenge. He braced the wrist against the edge of the bench and tried again, bare fingers scrabbling against the edge of the metal. The pain came instantly this time, a punishment for his efforts. It stabbed through tendon and muscle, a sharp, surgical burn that left him grinding his teeth just to stay upright. Uroboros flared again in pure defiance, flooding up his arm, trying again to swell beneath it and force it loose. It couldn’t cling. Couldn’t anchor. It slipped off and recoiled again with a ripple of pain that shot down through his ribcage. The backlash rattled his spine. Still, he kept going. Dug his thumb in, tried to wedge under it. Nothing. Tried to pull. Nothing. He rotated his wrist to the edge of the locker frame and slammed it once — then again. Then again. Metal shrieked and dented in. Skin split. Bone cracked. Blood smeared the frame. The Fog shifted, the injuries vanishing like they had never been there in the first place. The cuff remained untouched. He dropped to a knee, growling through the hurt, one hand braced against the wall, vision tunneling away from the sensation. For the first time in years, brute force had failed him completely. He straightened slowly, breathing through clenched teeth. The band glowed faintly with heat, offering consequences he had no counter for in the moment. He could try to knife his way under it, tissue damage be damned, but every metal undercut carried the risk of electronic lash and organ-straining bio-doses. There was no doubt anymore — even if he tried to remove the wrist entirely, the Fog would just grow it back. The station wasn’t his safe space anymore. He was never off duty now. And Herman was watching. The realization hit like a second blow: this wasn’t just restraint. It was ownership. A leash around his instincts. Around his choices. Around his life. He may as well have been back under Spencer’s thumb — a weapon in a glass box. But at least Spencer had been mortal. Predictable. Manipulable. This lunatic was something else entirely. Smarter.
